WRITE (2–3 sentences): I chose a logarithmic scale because the majority
of nc residents made less than 50k so using a log scale spreads those
income values out. Speading out those income values allows for viewers
to more easily distinguish how many residents make close to \$50,000 vs
those who make much less.

### A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3
#| ref.label: a3
#| echo: true

```

```{r}

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3

#| echo: false

```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (3–4 sentences): A fixed scale because it keeps the scale between
the male and female panels the same which lets viewers compare the rates
across the panels easier. This fixed scale, while allowing for easier
comparisons across panels, can mess up the scale of panels that have
different values, making comparisons inside panels slightly more
difficult.

WRITE (2–3 sentences): The clouds overlap heavily. Meaning that across

low means that a LARGE majority of NC residents have incomes below
\$25,000, which is off-putting considering that there are residents
making over \$500,000.

WRITE (2–4 sentences): Explain your colors. Say which column you colored
by and why. If your first choice failed the color check, say what you
changed: fewer categories, grouping rare ones, or panels. Then look at
your simulated plot: can you still tell the categories apart?

My colors go from blue to green and are colored by the marital_status
column because of the relatively low number of categories. This didn't
pass the color check, but was extremely close. So, I used the facet lump
to group together the smallest sections. After doing so, the color check
passed. After reducing the number of categories, it is extremely easy to
tell the categories apart.

```{r}
#| label: b1-check

```

WRITE (2 sentences): The plot shows the percentage of shots that
occurred in period 3. The most helpful label for first time viewers is
the labels of the groups on the y axis, showing views which groups is
and isn't period 3. This graph is interesting because it shows that, in
a hockey game, roughly 33% of shots occur in the final period, meaning
that there isn't an increase in shots taken as the game gets closer to
its end.

game_seconds_remaining because it's distribution is roughly even so a

made the graph harder to read for no reason.

### B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-b3
#| ref.label: b3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same plot in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "These plots show each period and the percentage that each shot outcome happend in that period"
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: b3-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (3–4 sentences): Fixed or free? What does the reader gain, and
what do they lose? Which panels are small, and what is their n?
Differences, not causes.

A fixed scale because it allows for easier comparisons across the
panels. They lose the ability to have a scale that best fits each panel
but we gain the ability to more easily compare each panel. And since all
the panels in the graph have similar proportions a fixed scales is more
beneficial than a free scale.

### B4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b4
#| ref.label: b4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "this plot shows the distance of each shot from the goal compared with if that shot was a goal or not."
```

```{r}
#| label: b4-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (2–3 sentences): The clouds overlap heavily the closer the shot
was to the goal. Meaning that the closer the shot happened to the goal
the more likely it was to score. The re-sampled means shows the average
distance from the goal that shots were taken for both shots that
resulted in goals, and all shots no matter the shot outcome, with shots
that resulted in goals being taken closer to the goal on average.
